t.2.40.1: The people, devoted to him, followed the great-souled Rāma, whose valour was true, as he set out to dwell in the forest.
t.2.40.2: Even when the circle of friends and the king had been forcibly made to turn back, those who had followed Rāma's chariot did not turn back at all.
t.2.40.3: For that greatly renowned one, endowed with virtues, was as dear to the men dwelling in Ayodhyā as the full moon.
t.2.40.4: Then Kākutstha, though entreated by his own subjects, making his father true to his word, went on to the forest all the same.
t.2.40.5: Gazing at them with affection, as though drinking them in with his eyes, Rāma spoke lovingly to those people as if they were his own children.
t.2.40.6: The affection and high esteem that the residents of Ayodhyā hold for me, let that be placed especially in Bharata, for the sake of what is dear to me.
t.2.40.7: For he, of virtuous conduct, who increases the joy of Kaikeyī, will rightly do for you what is pleasing and what is beneficial.
t.2.40.8: Mature in wisdom though young in years, gentle yet endowed with valour and virtues, he will be a fitting lord for you, one who dispels your fear.
t.2.40.9: For he, endowed with kingly virtues, has been chosen as crown prince; and moreover, instructed as you are by me, you must carry out the command of your lord.
t.2.40.10: And out of a wish to do what is dear to me, the great king must be so treated that he does not grieve when I have gone to dwell in the forest.
t.2.40.11: The more firmly the son of Daśaratha stood in dharma alone, the more the people longed for Rāma as their lord.
t.2.40.12: Rāma, together with Saumitri, seemed to draw along the dejected people, their faces veiled in tears, as though he had bound them with the cords of his virtues, pulling them back toward himself again as one draws back a seat.
t.2.40.13: Those twice-born men, venerable in three ways, in knowledge, in age and in spiritual power, their heads trembling with age, spoke these words from afar.
t.2.40.14: O you swift horses of noble breed who are carrying Rāma, turn back; you must not go on! Be devoted to the good of your master. Your master is one to be carried toward the city, not to be carried away from the city to the forest.
t.2.40.15: Seeing those aged brahmins lamenting thus with laments of distress, Rāma at once got down from his chariot.
t.2.40.16: Then Rāma, intent on the forest, went forth on foot, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, taking short and measured steps.
t.2.40.17: But Rāma, devoted to righteous conduct and with eyes full of compassion, could not bring himself to leave behind in his chariot those twice-born men who were following on foot.
t.2.40.18: Seeing Rāma going away even so, the twice-born, their minds bewildered and deeply anguished, spoke these words to Rāma.
t.2.40.19: This entire body of Brahmins follows you, who are devoted to Brahmins; and these sacred fires too, mounted upon the shoulders of the twice-born, go after you.
t.2.40.20: Behold these parasols of ours, obtained at the Vājapeya sacrifice, following behind you like swans at the close of the rainy season.
t.2.40.21: You have no parasol to shade you, and you are scorched by the sun's rays; we shall make shade for you with these very parasols of ours, earned at the Vājapeya sacrifice.
t.2.40.22: For our minds, which have always followed the mantras of the Veda, have for your sake, dear child, been turned to follow a life of dwelling in the forest.
t.2.40.23: The Vedas, which are our highest wealth, abide within our hearts; and our wives, guarded by their own good conduct, will remain right here in our homes.
t.2.40.24: No further deliberation need be made; the resolve to follow you has been well made. When you yourself are mindful of dharma, what need would there be for us to look to dharma?
t.2.40.25: O you of disciplined conduct, turn back, for we entreat you with our heads, their hair white as swans, and dusty from falling to the ground.
t.2.40.27: For all beings, moving and unmoving alike, are devoted to you; as they entreat you, show your affection to those who are devoted to you.
t.2.40.26: Many twice-born have begun sacrifices, and those sacrifices have come here with them; their completion, dear child, depends upon your turning back.
t.2.40.28: Unable to follow you, held back by their roots that restrain their eager rush, the trees, tossed upward by the force of the wind, seem to be crying aloud.
t.2.40.29: Even the birds, motionless, having given up their feeding and their roaming, and staying fixed in one place on the trees, entreat him who is compassionate toward all beings.
t.2.40.30: As those twice-born men were thus crying out for his return, it was seen there, through the darkness, that they seemed to be holding Rāghava back.
